before.text: Scrape your knee, and new skin soon grows over the wound.
Every one of those new skin cells carries the same 46 chromosomes as the cells around it.
So how does one cell split into two that match exactly?
Picture photocopying every page of a recipe book, then clipping each page to its copy.
Then you deal one page from every clipped pair into each of two binders.
In a cell, the pages are chromosomes, the clip is the centromere, and the binders are the two daughter cells.
Here is the whole path, from one cell on the left to two on the right.
It starts before mitosis, in interphase, when the cell copies all of its DNA.
A common mistake is to think mitosis itself does that copying.
But the copying is already done before mitosis begins, so mitosis only has to separate the copies.
First comes prophase: the chromosomes coil up thick, and spindle fibers grow from the two poles of the cell.
Up close, each chromosome is two identical sister chromatids, joined at the centromere.
That's one page clipped to its copy.
Spindle fibers from opposite poles attach at the centromere, one to each sister chromatid.
That matters, because now each copy will be pulled a different way.
Back on the path, metaphase comes next.
The spindle fibers line the chromosomes up single file across the middle of the cell.
Lined up like this, every chromosome is ready to split evenly between the two poles.
So what do you think happens when the fibers start to pull?
In anaphase, the centromere splits and the sister chromatids come apart.
The spindle fibers shorten, pulling each sister chromatid to the opposite pole.
That's the dealing, one page of every pair to each binder.
So each pole now holds one copy of every chromosome.
Back on the path, telophase builds a new nucleus around each set at the two poles.
Last, in cytokinesis, the cell pinches in two in the middle.
That leaves two daughter cells, each with the same complete set.
Now, what happens if one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase?
Both copies get pulled to the same pole.
So one daughter cell gets an extra chromosome, and the other is missing one.
The two cells no longer match, and they may not work properly.
That's why the cell checks that every chromosome is attached to spindle fibers before anaphase begins.
So a cell copies each chromosome, then spindle fibers pull one copy of each to opposite sides before splitting.
One cell with 46 chromosomes goes in, and two identical daughter cells with 46 each come out.
That's how a scraped knee fills with matching new skin.
